lines.say: Ten months later, a jury found her not guilty.
No one else was ever charged.
So who killed Andrew and Abby Borden?

shots.sub: A documentary investigation from the trial record

lines.say: In 1892, Fall River was a mill city. People called it Spindle City.
And Andrew Borden had made himself a wealthy man, in business, property and banking.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME

lines.say: He lived at 92 Second Street, with his second wife, Abby. They had married in 1865.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME

lower.title: 92 Second Street
lower.sub: Generic illustration, not the real house

lines.say: His two daughters from his first marriage lived there too. Emma, the elder. And Lizzie, who was thirty-two.
So did the family's maid, Bridget Sullivan. The sisters called her Maggie.
There was friction in the house, over property.
In 1887, Andrew bought a share of a house for Abby's half-sister, and put it in Abby's name. Emma later testified that it caused trouble in the family.
At the inquest, Lizzie said she had stopped calling Abby mother. Asked why, she said it was because she wanted to.
But Bridget testified that she never saw the two of them quarrel.
In the days before the killings, Andrew and Abby were sick to their stomachs.
Abby went to the family doctor, Seabury Bowen, and told him she was afraid they had been poisoned. He was sceptical.
The day before the killings, according to a drugstore clerk named Eli Bence, a woman he identified as Lizzie tried to buy prussic acid, a deadly poison.
The jury at her trial would never hear his story.
That day, Russell testified, Lizzie came to see her.
Russell testified that Lizzie told her: I feel afraid something is going to happen.
And Lizzie's uncle, John Morse, arrived unexpectedly, and stayed the night.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME

lines.say: Thursday, the fourth of August, was a hot day.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME

lines.say: Emma was away, visiting friends in Fairhaven, about fifteen miles off.
John Morse went out. He was visiting relatives when the killings happened.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME

lines.say: Andrew left at about nine, to do business downtown.
Abby asked Bridget to wash the windows, and Bridget spent much of the morning outside.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME

lines.say: At about half past nine, Abby went upstairs to tidy the guest room.
Within roughly the next hour, she was killed there.
Shortly before eleven, Andrew came home.
The front door was locked three ways. Bridget had to unlock it to let him in.
Bridget testified that as she fumbled with the locks, she said, pshaw, and heard Lizzie laugh, upstairs. She did not see her.
Andrew lay down on the sofa in the sitting room. Bridget went up to her attic room to rest. By her clock, she testified, it was eleven.
A few minutes after eleven, Lizzie called up to her. Her father was dead, she said. Somebody had come in and killed him.
A neighbour, Adelaide Churchill, came. So did the family doctor.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME

lines.say: Lizzie said Abby had gone out. A messenger had brought a note, she said, asking her to visit someone who was sick.
Neither the note, nor the messenger, was ever found.
Then, Bridget testified, Lizzie said she was almost sure she had heard Abby come back in.
Bridget would not go upstairs alone. Mrs. Churchill went with her. They found Abby in the guest room.
Medical evidence showed that Abby had died first, roughly an hour or more before her husband.
So where was Lizzie?
She told the neighbour and the doctor that she had gone out to the barn, for a piece of iron.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · HER ACCOUNT, AS SHE GAVE IT · GENERIC BARN

lines.say: At the inquest, she said she spent fifteen or twenty minutes up in the loft, looking for lead sinkers for a fishing trip. And she ate some pears.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · HER ACCOUNT, AS SHE GAVE IT · GENERIC BARN
ILLUSTRATION · HER ACCOUNT, AS SHE GAVE IT · GENERIC BARN

lines.say: Police said the loft was stifling hot, and that they found no footprints there to back up her story.
But a defence witness, an ice cream peddler named Hyman Lubinsky, testified that shortly after eleven he saw a woman walk from the barn toward the house.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL HOME
ILLUSTRATION · AN UNIDENTIFIED WOMAN, AS DESCRIBED

lines.say: And at the inquest, her answers shifted. She said she was on the stairs. Then in the kitchen. Then perhaps the dining room.
In the basement, police found a hatchet head. Its handle had been broken off.
The prosecution could never prove it was the murder weapon.
The inquest ran from the ninth to the eleventh of August. Lizzie testified without a lawyer.
On the eleventh, she was arrested. The next day she pleaded not guilty, and she was taken to the jail in Taunton.
Which brings us back to that Sunday morning, in the kitchen.
Russell testified that Lizzie was at the stove with a dress, and that Emma was in the room.

depicts.act: holding a dress at the kitchen stove

lines.say: Lizzie said she was going to burn this old thing up. It was covered with paint.
Russell said she told Lizzie she would not let anyone see her do that.
But Russell also testified that she saw no blood on the dress, and never actually saw it go into the stove.

shots.title: What she did not see
items: Not the dress going into the stove

lines.say: Emma testified that it was an old dress, stained with paint soon after it was made that May. When Lizzie said she would burn it, Emma's answer, she said, was: do it.
Russell testified that she had not mentioned the dress at the early hearings.
And at first, the grand jury did not indict Lizzie.
Then, on the first of December, Russell went back and told them about the dress. The next day, Lizzie was indicted for murder.
Prosecutors said the dress was burned to cover up the crime. The defence said it was burned in broad daylight, in front of witnesses.

THE DEFENCE
body: an old dress, burned in daylight

lines.say: The trial opened in New Bedford on the fifth of June, 1893.
Newspapers all over the country, and beyond, followed it.
Three judges sat on the case. The jury was twelve men.
Lizzie's lead lawyer was George Robinson, a former governor of Massachusetts.
And as governor, Robinson had appointed one of the three judges.
One of the prosecutors, William Moody, would later sit on the United States Supreme Court.

rows.text: became a U.S. Supreme Court justice.

lines.say: Two things never reached the jury: Lizzie's inquest testimony, and the drugstore clerk's poison story. The judges kept both out.
Lizzie never took the stand.
In his charge to the jury, Justice Dewey stressed the presumption of innocence, and the gaps in the state's case. One newspaper said it was a plea for the innocent.

shots.sub: A newspaper's verdict on the judge's charge

lines.say: On the twentieth of June, the jury went out.
Accounts differ on how long they took. About an hour. Some say an hour and a half.
Not guilty.
Lizzie and Emma inherited their father's fortune.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL MAPLECROFT

lines.say: They bought a big house in one of the best neighbourhoods in town, and Lizzie named it Maplecroft.

shots.label: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC HOUSE, NOT THE REAL MAPLECROFT

lines.say: She began calling herself Lizbeth.
But much of Fall River shunned her for the rest of her life.
In 1905, Emma moved out. The sisters never reconciled.
Lizzie died on the first of June, 1927. Emma died nine days later.
In her will, Lizzie left money to the Animal Rescue League.

rows.text: Lizzie left part of her estate

lines.say: So who killed Andrew and Abby Borden?
Prosecutors argued that it was Lizzie. She was at home. She burned a dress. A clerk said she had tried to buy poison, though the jury never heard that.
Historians have argued that her class, and the fact that she was a woman, help explain why she was not convicted.
But no blood was found on her, no weapon was proven, and the jury that heard the evidence acquitted her.
Writers have pointed at others: at Bridget, at John Morse, at Emma, at an unknown intruder.
There is no direct evidence against Bridget. Morse had an alibi. Emma was miles away.

head: THE THEORY
THE RECORD
body: no direct evidence · an alibi · in Fairhaven

lines.say: In 2012, the journals of Lizzie's own lawyer surfaced. They had sat for years in his attic, in a Victorian bathtub.

lines.say: Today, the house on Second Street is a museum, and a bed and breakfast. You can stay the night.

lines.say: This autumn, a Netflix drama sent Lizzie Borden to number one all over again. This film has kept to the record.
Lizzie Borden was acquitted. No one else was ever charged. And more than a hundred and thirty years later, the question is still open.
